Chapter 3: Expanding the Capacity for Positive Energy and Joy.
So, now that we’ve uncovered those hidden roots of self-sabotage, what’s next? Well, it’s time to actively grow your ability to welcome happiness, love, and real success into your life.
And no, this isn’t about pretending everything’s perfect or sweeping your struggles under the rug. It’s about learning how to actually allow yourself to feel good, sometimes even for the very first time.
You know, it’s surprisingly common to feel more comfortable when things are tough, or when you’re struggling. Ever noticed how, when life starts going really well, there’s a little voice that says, “Wait, this can’t last,” or you suddenly look for something—anything—to worry about? That’s called the Upper Limit Problem. It’s like an invisible thermostat, keeping your joy and success within a range that feels familiar, even if it’s not what you truly want.
So, how do you expand your capacity for positive energy?
First, start by simply noticing and accepting good feelings when they show up. Maybe you get a genuine compliment, or you share a laugh with a friend, or you accomplish something you’ve been working on. Instead of brushing these moments off, try to pause and actually let yourself feel the happiness. Savor it—even if it feels a little awkward at first.
Next, if positive feelings make you nervous or uncomfortable, don’t run from them. Instead, take a few slow, deep breaths. Let that feeling settle in. This helps your body and mind get used to new levels of well-being, rather than snapping back to old habits.
And when those old stories pop up—like, “I don’t deserve this,” or “Something bad’s bound to happen”—gently challenge them. Remind yourself that it’s safe to feel good. You don’t have to earn happiness, and you certainly don’t have to justify it.
Here’s another important practice: welcoming abundance. That means saying yes to opportunities, to help, and to love. If you notice yourself deflecting a compliment or downplaying your achievements, pause and try accepting them with gratitude. It might feel strange at first, but with time, it gets easier.
Think of your ability to feel happiness as a container. For many of us, this container started out pretty small, shaped by our past experiences and beliefs. The goal isn’t to make it perfect, but to slowly expand it—so it can hold more and more positive energy without overflowing or spilling out.
Every time you allow yourself to feel a little more happiness or success, your container grows. And over time, you’ll notice it becomes much easier to experience real joy, genuine connection, and lasting fulfillment—without that urge to self-sabotage.
Remember, this is a practice. It takes patience, kindness toward yourself, and a willingness to stretch beyond what’s familiar. But with each step, your life becomes richer, more vibrant, and closer to the potential that’s always been yours.
